newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Strong Russia buying sees premium on T-bill sale.
newsitem.headline: Strong Russia buying sees premium on T-bill sale.

text.p: Aggressive local buying led to a premium over market yields at an auction of 346-day GKO discount Treasury bills on Wednesday, while foreign investors showed little interest in the sales, dealers said.
The Finance Ministry sold 714-day T-bills with a yield of 31.08 percent at the first auction.
It also sold a 161-day T-bill with a yield of 28.31 percent at the second auction.

"The first auction gave us a yield higher than the market one because many dealers bid in large lots counting on 31 percent yield," said Tokobank dealer Tatyana Lutseva. "At the second auction the yield was lower than the market one as most bids were non-competitive ones."
On Tuesday the average market yield was 28.6 percent.
Dealers said foreign investors had lost interest in long-term issues as they already have big portfolios of such paper.

"Maybe it is an alarm bell that the price rise will not be endless," said Stanislav Litvinov, a dealer from Natsionalny Rezervny Bank. "Although the trend is unlikely to change, most likely it will be slower."
Yevgeny Krayev, a dealer from International Moscow Bank, said foreigners were more interested in the shorter issue as the current yield level suited them no longer.
"It is clear that non-residents do not invest in papers on which the Central Bank's policy is not clear," he said.

"No one quotes forwards for them for after the New Year and there are few investors who would like to speculate on one-year issues. Those who wanted to speculate on long-term issues have already made their investment."

The Central Bank has said it would cut the required length of forwards and options for non-residents repatriating funds from about four months at present to nothing by the end of the year, as it liberalises the market.

Under the current system the Central Bank quotes its own forward rates for these deals, although the central bank rates are used only for a part of the transaction, while the remainder is already based on commercial bank rates.
Dealers forecast a slight price rise at Thursday's trading due to investors' unwillingness to sell paper ahead of the long weekend. Russian markets are closed May 9-11.
